title: Endocrine system
summary: Hormones, endocrine glands and how the body is regulated by chemical signals
cards.0.p: A hormone is a chemical messenger that a gland releases directly into the blood. Endocrine glands have no ducts. Exocrine glands release their secretions through a duct. Mixed glands do both.
cards.0.key: If a gland has no duct, its secretion goes into the blood and the gland is endocrine. If it has a duct, the gland is exocrine. The pancreas and the sex glands are mixed glands.
cards.0.once.soru: A sweat gland releases its secretion onto the skin through a duct. What kind of gland is it?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: A gland that releases its secretion onto a body surface through a duct is an exocrine gland.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: An endocrine gland has no duct, and its secretion goes directly into the blood.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: A mixed gland releases secretions both into the blood and into a duct. A sweat gland releases only into a duct.
cards.1.h: What all hormones have in common
cards.1.p: A hormone travels through the whole body in the blood, but it only affects target cells that have the right receptor. Even a tiny amount is enough. Hormones are broken down in the liver and removed by the kidneys.
cards.1.svg#1: the hormone travels everywhere in the blood
cards.1.key: The same hormone can have different effects on different targets. For example, adrenaline speeds up the heart but slows down digestion.
cards.2.p: Hormones fall into three groups by structure. Insulin and ADH are proteins or peptides, adrenaline and thyroxine are amines, and cortisol and the sex hormones are steroids. Steroids pass through the membrane, and their receptors are inside the cell.
cards.2.key: Steroid hormones are made in the smooth ER, and protein hormones are made by ribosomes. Protein hormones and adrenaline have their receptors on the membrane. Thyroxine enters the cell.
cards.2.once.soru: Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol. Can they pass easily through the cell membrane?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Steroids are fat-soluble. So they pass directly through the lipid layer of the membrane.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The ones that cannot pass through the membrane are protein hormones, and their receptors are on the membrane.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Steroids cross the membrane without needing a carrier.
cards.3.p: The nervous system sends messages through neurons. This is fast, short-lived and goes to a specific target. The endocrine system sends messages through the blood. This is slow, long-lasting and affects a wide area. The hypothalamus links the two systems.
cards.3.svg#17: the bridge between the two systems: hypothalamus
cards.3.key: Pulling your hand away from a hot stove is nervous control. Growing taller is hormonal control.
cards.4.p: The hypothalamus releases TRH, the pituitary releases TSH, and TSH stimulates the thyroid. When thyroxine rises in the blood, TRH and TSH fall. This is called negative feedback. The product puts the brakes on its own production.
cards.4.svg#8: when thyroxine rises, TRH and TSH fall
cards.4.key: This system works like a thermostat. Oxytocin during childbirth is an example of positive feedback.
cards.5.h: The hypothalamus and the posterior pituitary
cards.5.p: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary. ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary and released into the blood from there. ADH increases water reabsorption in the kidneys. Oxytocin contracts the uterus during childbirth.
cards.5.svg#7: ADH → more water reabsorbed in the kidney
cards.5.svg#8: oxytocin → uterus contracts, milk is let down
cards.5.key: The posterior pituitary does not make hormones. It stores and releases the hormones made by the hypothalamus. Oxytocin also lets milk flow during breastfeeding.
cards.5.once.soru: You lost a lot of water and you are thirsty. How do your kidneys adjust your urine?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: ADH rises and the kidney reabsorbs water. So urine becomes less and darker.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: This happens when the body has too much water.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The kidney constantly adjusts urine to the body's water balance.
cards.6.h: The anterior pituitary: manager of the glands
cards.6.p: The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones. GH drives growth. TSH stimulates the thyroid, ACTH the adrenal cortex, and FSH and LH the sex glands. Prolactin drives milk production.
cards.6.key: Prolactin makes milk, and oxytocin lets it flow. ACTH stands for adrenocorticotropic hormone, FSH for follicle-stimulating hormone and LH for luteinizing hormone.
cards.6.once.soru: The anterior pituitary also controls other glands. If it is damaged, what happens to the thyroid?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The TSH that stimulates the thyroid stops coming, and thyroxine falls.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: When its signal stops, a gland does not speed up. It slows down.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The thyroid works on the TSH released by the anterior pituitary.
cards.7.p: The thyroid releases the hormone thyroxine, which contains iodine, and thyroxine sets the metabolic rate. If there is not enough iodine, the gland grows. This is called a goiter. Using iodized salt prevents goiter.
cards.7.key: Too much thyroxine (hyperthyroidism) causes weight loss and a racing heart. Too little thyroxine (hypothyroidism) causes tiredness and weight gain. Thyroxine is essential for growth and brain development in childhood.
cards.8.p: The parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone. When blood Ca2+ falls, parathyroid hormone releases calcium from bone. When Ca2+ rises, the thyroid releases calcitonin, which sends calcium into bone.
cards.8.key: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium, and calcitonin lowers it. These two hormones have opposite (antagonistic) effects. Parathyroid hormone also increases calcium reabsorption in the kidney and absorption in the intestine.
cards.8.once.soru: Blood calcium has dropped. What happens to the calcium in the bones?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Parathyroid hormone releases calcium from bone, and blood calcium rises.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Calcium is sent into bone by calcitonin when blood levels are high.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Bone is the body's calcium store, and this store is used when calcium levels fall.
cards.9.p: The cortex of the adrenal gland releases cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol raises blood sugar under stress, and aldosterone makes the body hold on to Na+ and water. The medulla of the gland releases adrenaline.
cards.9.svg#0: cross section of the adrenal gland
cards.9.key: The adrenal medulla is stimulated by sympathetic nerves. Adrenaline is the response to sudden danger, and cortisol is the response to long-lasting stress.
cards.9.once.soru: You hear a noise in the dark at night, you jump and your heart races. Which hormone causes this?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: In sudden danger, the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and the heart speeds up.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Insulin lowers blood sugar. It does not speed up the heart.
cards.10.p: The endocrine part of the pancreas is called the islets of Langerhans. After a meal, β cells release insulin and blood sugar falls. When you are hungry, α cells release glucagon and blood sugar rises.
cards.10.key: Insulin is the only hormone that lowers blood sugar. Glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise it. The liver and muscles store glucose as glycogen.
cards.11.p: If insulin is missing or does not work, blood sugar rises and sugar passes into the urine. This is called diabetes. In type 1 diabetes, the β cells are destroyed. In type 2 diabetes, cells do not respond to insulin.
cards.11.svg#14: in both: high blood sugar, sugar in urine,
cards.11.key: In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the β cells. In type 2 diabetes, the problem is not a lack of insulin but insulin resistance. Excess weight raises this risk.
cards.11.once.soru: A patient's pancreas cannot make insulin. What happens to their blood sugar?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Without insulin, cells cannot take in glucose, so glucose stays in the blood.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The hormone that lowers blood sugar is insulin. Without insulin, sugar does not fall.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: There is no other hormone that lowers blood sugar.
cards.12.h: Sex glands, the pineal gland and the thymus
cards.12.p: The testes release testosterone, and the ovaries release estrogen and progesterone. The pineal gland releases melatonin in the dark and sets the sleep cycle. T lymphocytes mature in the thymus.
cards.12.key: Sex hormones control the sex traits that appear at puberty. The thymus shrinks after puberty. The menstrual cycle is covered in the Reproductive system topic.
cards.12.once.soru: You look at a bright screen for a long time before bed. Why is your sleep delayed?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: Melatonin rises in the dark, and screen light suppresses it.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Insulin regulates blood sugar, not sleep.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: A drop in adrenaline makes falling asleep easier, not harder.
cards.13.p: In childhood, too much GH causes gigantism and too little causes dwarfism. In adults, too much GH causes acromegaly. A lack of thyroxine causes congenital hypothyroidism, and a lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.
cards.13.key: Congenital hypothyroidism causes delayed growth and intellectual disability in childhood. In diabetes insipidus, large amounts of diluted urine are produced.
cards.13.etk.soru: Match each disorder with its cause.
cards.13.etk.ciftler.2.1: Too much GH in an adult
cards.13.once.soru: If an adult has too much GH, do they grow taller?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: In adults the growth plates have closed. So the hands, feet and jaw get thicker instead.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Height increases only while the growth plates are open, that is, in childhood.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: After the growth plates close, height does not increase at all.
cards.14.p: The stomach increases acid secretion with the hormone gastrin. The small intestine triggers bicarbonate release with the hormone secretin. An empty stomach releases ghrelin, which makes you hungry. Fat tissue releases leptin, which tells the brain "the stores are full".
cards.14.key: When the response to leptin weakens, it is harder to feel full. This contributes to obesity and raises the risk of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.
cards.14.once.soru: How does fat tissue send the "stores are full" message to the brain?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fat tissue releases leptin, and leptin reaches the brain through the blood.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Fat tissue sends this message through the blood, not through nerves.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Fat tissue can also release hormones.
cards.15.p:
• Endocrine glands have no ducts. A hormone travels in the blood and affects its target cell.
• Hormonal effects start slowly, last long and affect a wide area.
• The hypothalamus and pituitary control the other glands. Negative feedback keeps the balance.
• Insulin and glucagon have opposite effects, and so do calcitonin and parathyroid hormone.
quiz.0.q: Match each hormone with where it is released.
quiz.0.e: Insulin is released by the β cells of the islets of Langerhans, and parathyroid hormone by the parathyroid glands. Cortisol comes from the cortex of the adrenal gland, and adrenaline from its medulla. Melatonin is the hormone of the pineal gland.
quiz.1.q: Group each hormone by its chemical structure.
quiz.1.e: Insulin, GH and ADH are proteins or peptides. Adrenaline, thyroxine and melatonin are amines derived from amino acids. Cortisol and aldosterone are steroids derived from cholesterol.
quiz.2.q: Put in order the chain that sets the cortisol level during long-lasting stress.
quiz.2.ogeler.0: The hypothalamus releases a releasing hormone
quiz.2.ogeler.3: Cortisol puts the brakes on the hypothalamus and pituitary
quiz.2.e: This chain works on the same logic as the TRH-TSH-thyroxine chain. The hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary, and ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex. Rising cortisol puts the brakes on the chain. This is called negative feedback.
quiz.3.q: A healthy student's blood sugar rises above normal after lunch and returns to normal within two hours. What mainly brings it down?
quiz.3.e: When blood sugar rises, β cells release insulin. Cells take in glucose and the liver stores glycogen. Glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise blood sugar.
quiz.3.y.0: Glucagon raises blood sugar. The hormone that lowers sugar after a meal is insulin.
quiz.3.y.2: Adrenaline raises blood sugar. The hormone that lowers it by moving sugar into cells is insulin.
quiz.3.y.3: Cortisol raises blood sugar. The drop after a meal comes from insulin released by the pancreas.
A:ozet: See which cells a hormone affects, race nervous control against hormonal control, balance blood sugar with insulin and watch the thyroid's brake.
A:adimlar.0.metin: A hormone spreads through the whole body in the blood. Some cells have receptors on their surface that recognize it. Press play and see which cells respond.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: In which cells does the hormone have an effect?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The hormone reaches every cell, but a cell without the receptor does not recognize it.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The hormone binds to its receptor like a key in a lock. A cell without the receptor is not affected.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Because the hormone travels in the blood, it can affect faraway cells too.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The nervous system and the endocrine system work together, but at different speeds. Race the effects of the two systems.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A hormone arrives slowly in the blood, but it stays there for a while. So its effect starts late and lasts long.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A nervous effect starts very fast but does not last long.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Their durations are clearly different. The nervous effect is short, and the hormonal effect is long.
A:adimlar.2.metin: After a meal, blood sugar rises and the β cells of the pancreas release insulin. Play it first without insulin, then turn insulin on.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Turn insulin on and play again.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: Insulin let the cells take in glucose, and the liver stored the extra glucose as glycogen. So blood sugar returned to normal.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Blood sugar is normally kept at about 70-110 mg/dL. Change the blood sugar and watch how the pancreas responds.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: After a long fast, blood sugar fell to 60 mg/dL. Which hormone is released?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Insulin lowers blood sugar. It is not released when sugar is already low.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The α cells of the pancreas release glucagon. The liver then breaks down glycogen and releases glucose into the blood.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: ADH is released from the pituitary and increases water reabsorption in the kidney. It does not regulate blood sugar.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The hypothalamus releases TRH, the pituitary releases TSH, and TSH tells the thyroid to make thyroxine. Raise the thyroxine and watch the hormones above it.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: As thyroxine rose, TRH and TSH fell. This is called negative feedback. The product puts the brakes on the chain that makes it, so its level stays steady.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The thyroid uses iodine to make thyroxine. Turn on iodine deficiency and see what happens to the chain.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Why does the thyroid grow (goiter) when iodine is lacking?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The problem is a lack of iodine, not too much.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Without iodine, thyroxine cannot be made, so thyroxine falls.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: When thyroxine falls, the hypothalamus and pituitary are no longer braked. The rising TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid and the gland grows.
A:kapanis.0: A hormone travels everywhere in the blood, but it only affects cells that have its receptor.
A:kapanis.1: Nervous effects are fast and short, while hormonal effects are slow and long-lasting.
A:kapanis.2: Insulin lowers blood sugar, and glucagon raises it.
A:kapanis.3: Thyroxine puts the brakes on TRH and TSH. This is called negative feedback.
A:kapanis.4: With iodine deficiency this brake is lost, TSH rises and a goiter forms.
